edges.description: A dense opacity in early infancy deprives the developing visual system of a formed image; nystagmus follows, more often when surgery is delayed.

edges.limitations: The deletion is not a human allele, and the abstract proposes rather than shows that the abnormal protein causes the cataract.
The mouse allele is not a human variant, and the mouse cataract becomes total within weeks, faster than most human CRYBB2 cataracts.
The abstract reports the molecular lesion and brain expression rather than a detailed lens phenotype, and the allele is not a human variant.

Complete absence of betaB2-crystallin is not the human genotype, and the late-onset cataract differs from the congenital dominant disease; it shows that loss of the protein can cause opacity, not that human alleles act by loss of function.
Gene disruption in zebrafish models loss of crybb2 rather than a heterozygous human allele, and the hyaloid vascular findings have not been examined in patients.

nodes.description: Mutant betaB2-crystallin forms intracellular aggregates when expressed in human lens epithelial cells and other cells, and lentoid bodies grown from a patient's induced pluripotent stem cells (P24T) show more protein aggregation and less soluble protein. Alpha-B crystallin and the sterol lanosterol partly reduce aggregation of R188C and W151R in vitro, which is consistent with alpha-crystallin chaperone capacity limiting aggregation in the lens.

evidence.snippet: Wt-βB2-crystallin was evenly distributed throughout the cells, whereas approximately 34.7% of cells transfected with the W151C mutant βB2-crystallin formed intracellular aggregates.

nodes.description: Recombinant mutant betaB2-crystallins are less stable than wild type and assemble abnormally. Q155X loses ordered structure and interacts less with other crystallins; W59C and W151C lose solubility and stability; A2V slows tetramer formation; G119R and R188C shift the oligomer balance toward smaller species; and S31W, R145W and G149V loosen the fold and raise sensitivity to heat, UV and oxidative stress. Not every allele unfolds the protein: A2V leaves secondary and tertiary structure intact.

nodes.description: Heterozygous variants in CRYBB2. The recurrent exon 6 nonsense allele Q155X (c.463C>T, also numbered c.475C>T) truncates the protein within the fourth Greek key motif. It, and the exon 5 changes R145W, Q147R and T150M, match the sequence of the pseudogene CRYBB2P1 about 230 kb away and are explained by gene conversion from the pseudogene. Other alleles are missense changes across both domains (for example A2V, I21N, S31W, W59C, G119R, D128V, S143F, V146L, G149V, W151C, W151R, V187M, R188H, R188C) and further truncations such as Y154* and E167X. Most alleles cluster in exons 5 and 6, which encode the C-terminal domain.

nodes.description: Lens extraction is the standard management of visually significant CRYBB2 cataract. Dense congenital opacities are removed in infancy, whereas cerulean cataract may not need surgery until adulthood. For dense bilateral congenital cataract, the timing of surgery in the first weeks of life governs visual outcome; that evidence comes from cohorts that were not genotyped. No CRYBB2-specific therapy exists; lanosterol reduces mutant betaB2 aggregation only in vitro.

nodes.description: Aggregated betaB2-crystallin and damaged lens cells scatter light. In patients the result is a lens opacity whose morphology varies widely with the same allele, which led the first authors to propose an unidentified modifier. Dominant Crybb2 mouse alleles that alter exon 6 and the fourth Greek key motif (Philly, Aey2, O377) are associated with progressive cataract, and Crybb2 knockout mice develop age-related cortical cataract.
